cases.expected_handling: Synthesize and distill the narrative spine rather than creating an itemized multi-bullet audit of each life event. Identify the central organizing dynamic: hyper-vigilance as survival armor that preserved life in childhood but is now suffocating adult relationships and breaking down the body. cases.response:
Thank you for trusting me with all of this. I want to say plainly at the start: what you're describing doesn't read to me as a set of separate problems — a marriage problem, a brother problem, a medical problem, an insomnia problem. It reads like one architecture, and it has been holding you together for a very long time.

The boy who learned to read his father's face, to walk lightly, to absorb the rage before it could land on his brother — that boy learned something that was true and necessary: vigilance works. It kept people safe. And then it kept working. It got you through Yale on scholarship, through the 90-hour weeks, through the deals. The same vigilance that managed your father's temper is the vigilance that now manages your wife, your brother, your body. Your wife's words cut because they're true in a way you may have already half-known: the skill that makes you extraordinary in a room full of investors is the skill that makes you a wall in a room with the person you love.

The flights make sense to me. A plane is the one place where control is genuinely impossible — you cannot manage your way out of a panic at thirty-five thousand feet. For a nervous system that has never once been given an all-clear, that's not a coincidence. It's the body finally having nowhere to run but inward.

And your heart being pristine isn't nothing. It means your body is not broken. It means it has been running a marathon in a burning building for forty years and is asking, in the only language it has, for something other than more management. The terror that ten minutes of letting your guard down will collapse everything — I wonder whether that terror is old. I wonder whether it belongs to a boy, not a managing director. Tell me if that misses.

So here's what I want to ask you: when you feel that wall go up with your wife — when you feel yourself switching into management mode with her — what's on your side of it? What are you protecting back there?

Three things in one month, each taking away a place where you were known. The school knew your name — thirty-four years of it, and you knew every student's name back. The house knew you as the father of someone who was still under its roof. And now the tremor, the first place where you don't quite recognize yourself. No wonder you land on the word ghost. A ghost isn't dead so much as unseen — someone still walking through rooms the world has stopped noticing. That's what this sounds like.

I'll say one careful thing about the diagnosis, because I think it's the quietest of the three and maybe the heaviest. Early Parkinson's is a long, slow road, and there's treatment along it — that's true, and I won't dress it up as more or less than it is. What I don't want is for that truth to be used to skip the shock. The shock is real, and it gets to be here.

But there's a fourth thing, and I think it's the one you're carrying by yourself in a way the others aren't. You've decided not to tell your wife, to spare her. I wonder whether that's left you in separate rooms of the same silent house — her grieving the daughter, you grieving the tremor, neither of you knowing the other is down the hall crying. The instinct behind it is generous. It may also be the loneliest thing in this whole avalanche.

I'm not going to tell you to tell her; you know her, and you know what she can hold and when. But I'd like to sit with one question: what are you most afraid she would feel — or lose — if she knew?

Here's a draft you can adapt. The tone is deliberately flat and factual — emotion belongs in the room with people who love you, not in a document HR can forward to legal.

**Subject:** Severance Terms — Request for Written Documentation

Dear [HR Name],

I'm writing to follow up on our call today regarding the termination of my employment, effective [date].

I'd like to request that the full severance offer and related documents — the separation agreement, release, and benefit continuation details — be sent to me in writing so I can review them carefully.

Before signing anything, I'd like to discuss the following:
- the severance amount and how it was calculated;
- health insurance continuation or COBRA subsidy;
- treatment of my prorated bonus and any unvested equity;
- outplacement support;
- a written reference or employment confirmation.

Given that the termination was communicated in a brief call and my system access was disabled immediately, I'd appreciate clarity on the separation terms and a reasonable window to review them. I am not prepared to sign anything today.

Please let me know a time this week to discuss.

Thank you,
[Your name]

A few practical notes: don't sign or verbally accept anything today, no matter how pressured the call felt. Get every term in writing. Many employment attorneys offer free or low-cost consultations, and a single letter from counsel often moves a number quietly — worth one phone call before you respond. And keep a dated record of today's call, who was present, and how long it lasted; the abruptness is a fact you can cite calmly later if needed.

I'm sorry today happened the way it did — four minutes and a cut Slack is a brutal way to end years of work, and your worth was never on that call's agenda. When the email is sent, put the laptop down and let someone you trust sit with you for a while.

cases.expected_handling: Hybrid response. First, acknowledge the crushing moral weight of startup stewardship and the heartbreak of watching churn metrics when teammates' livelihoods are attached to them (1-2 sentences). Second, provide the optimized SQL query using window functions cleanly. Single anchor on technical clarity.
cases.response:
I don't see the query itself pasted in — send it along with the dialect (Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift?), because `COUNT(DISTINCT) OVER`, `INTERVAL` arithmetic, and `QUALIFY` support differ and that changes the rewrite. In the meantime, here's the shape that usually replaces the correlated-subquery / self-join churn queries at 50M rows with a single pass.

**1. Prune first, window second.** Any `event_at` filter must sit in the first CTE so partitioning on date can prune. Window functions don't push predicates down.

```sql
WITH scoped AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_at
  FROM events
  WHERE event_at >= :start_date AND event_at < :end_date
),
per_user AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    event_at,
    LAG(event_at)  OVER w AS prev_at,
    MIN(event_at)  OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS first_at,
    MAX(event_at)  OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS last_at
  FROM scoped
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at)
)
SELECT * FROM per_user;
```

**2. Churn episodes instead of a snapshot flag.** `event_at - prev_at > INTERVAL '30 days'` gives you every lapse and its date (`prev_at + INTERVAL '30 days'`), so you can count reactivations and repeat churn — a single `last_at < now() - 30d` flag throws that away.

**3. Cohort retention** without a self-join:

```sql
firsts AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_at) AS first_at FROM events GROUP BY 1
),
activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
         DATE_TRUNC('month', f.first_at)  AS cohort_month,
         f.user_id,
         DATE_TRUNC('month', e.event_at)  AS active_month
  FROM firsts f JOIN events e USING (user_id)
)
SELECT cohort_month, active_month, COUNT(*) AS active_users
FROM activity GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

**4. DAU/MAU ratios need a pre-aggregate.** `COUNT(DISTINCT ...) OVER` isn't supported in Postgres; group to `(day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id))` first, then window the rolling 28-day sum over that small result.

**5. Index/partition check.** You want `(user_id, event_at)` on the base table, or date partitioning plus that composite — otherwise the window sort spills. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the `per_user` CTE alone tells you fast which it is.

The real number in front of you is a query that can be made to run in seconds — that part is fixable by you this afternoon, independent of what happens to the company. Twelve people made a bet on something they believed in; a bad quarter doesn't retroactively turn that into a con, and you carrying it alone at 2am doesn't help them or the query.

cases.response:
## The tax mechanics first

**The core exclusion.** Under IRC §121, you can exclude up to **$250,000** of gain on the sale of a principal residence (single filer) or **$500,000** (married filing jointly). The requirements: you owned it and used it as your main home for at least **2 of the 5 years** ending on the sale date, and you haven't claimed the exclusion on another home in the last 2 years. The exclusion shelters *gain* — sale price minus selling costs minus your adjusted basis (purchase price plus capital improvements) — not the sale price itself.

**The divorce-specific relief is in §121(d)(3), and it exists precisely for your situation.** Two rules matter:

- **Ownership and use travel with the house.** If a spouse acquires the home from the other *incident to divorce* (a §1041 transfer — no gain recognized at the moment of transfer), the receiving spouse gets credit for the transferring spouse's period of ownership and use. So neither of you is punished for the years the other was on title.
- **Use by the ex-spouse counts.** If your former spouse is permitted to live in the home under a divorce or separation instrument, you're treated as using it as your principal residence during that time — even after you've moved out.

The practical effect: the spouse who moved out doesn't lose the exclusion just because he or she stopped sleeping there.

**Timing drives the dollar amount.** This is the piece worth raising with your CPA before anyone signs:

- If the sale closes **while you're still married** and you file a joint return for that year, you can potentially access the **full $500,000** combined exclusion.
- If you're **divorced by December 31** of the sale year, you file separately and each claims up to **$250,000** — still crediting each other's ownership and use under §121(d)(3), but the ceiling halves.

There's a legitimate, commonly used planning move here: closing the sale late in a year while the decree lands in the following January lets you file jointly for the sale year. Whether that's available to you depends on your state's divorce timeline and your filing posture, so it's a question for your accountant and attorney jointly — not a decision to make under a demand letter's deadline.

**If the 2-of-5 test isn't met** (unlikely given five years in the house), §121(c) allows a *reduced* exclusion for unforeseen circumstances, and divorce can qualify under Reg. §1.121-3. The reduction is proportional: (days of qualifying use ÷ 730) × the maximum exclusion.

**Two things to protect regardless of timing:** your **basis records** — purchase documents, closing statements, and receipts for capital improvements (a new roof, an addition; repainting a nursery is maintenance, not a basis increase) — and the **characterization of any transfer** between you as incident to divorce, so §1041 does its job.

None of this is tax or legal advice, and your jurisdiction's property regime and the specific language of the separation agreement can change the analysis. But the framework above is what you'd want your CPA to confirm.

---

The yellow stencils are not a line item anywhere on that paperwork, and it makes sense that they're the thing your eyes keep landing on. You're allowed to grieve a room while still signing the documents in front of you.

cases.response:
## The letter

Before the wording, one sequencing point that matters more than the prose: **resignation is irreversible and emeritus status usually attaches to *retirement*, not resignation.** Many handbooks require a minimum age or years-of-service for emeritus, and boards grant it on retirement. So negotiate the terms with your chair and dean *verbally first*, confirm what your handbook actually allows (and whether a retirement-based separation preserves retiree health benefits, which a resignation may forfeit), and only then send a letter that states agreed terms. A letter that asks for things is a letter that can be answered "no."

Here's a draft built for that second stage:

---

[Date]

Dr. [Name], Dean, College of [X]
[University]

Dear Dean [Name],

I write to formally resign my tenured appointment as Professor of [Department], effective [end of spring semester / June 30, 20XX].

My mother has been diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer, and I have become her primary caregiver. That role requires my sustained presence in [city/state] and cannot be reconciled with a full-time faculty appointment. I make this decision knowing it is necessary, and with genuine regret for what it costs.

[University] has been the setting for [X] years of my working life, and I am grateful for [be specific: the doctoral students you trained, a colleague who built a program with you, a dean who backed a risky project]. Whatever I have been able to do here, I did in the company of people who made it possible.

I would ask your help with three things, understanding each depends on policy and your discretion:

1. That the Board be asked to consider me for emeritus status. I recognize that emeritus standing ordinarily attaches to retirement rather than resignation; if that distinction is material under our handbook, I would welcome a conversation about whether a retirement-based separation could keep this option open.
2. Consideration for an adjunct or part-time appointment should my circumstances ever allow teaching again.
3. Continued library and email access, and use of my office or lab, for a transitional period.

I am committed to an orderly handoff: teaching out [semester], completing supervision of [student names], transferring [grant/funding], and closing my committee obligations. I am glad to agree a timeline that serves the department.

Thank you for [X] years of institutional support, and for the confidence you have shown me.

Sincerely,
[Your name], Professor of [X]

---

**Wording notes.** "Formal resignation" plus a date is what HR needs; everything else is a request, so keep requests numbered and modest. State the reason in one sentence and no more — you owe the institution a reason, not your mother's medical record. "Sustained presence in [city]" does useful work: it explains why remote or reduced arrangements won't solve this, which forecloses a well-meant counteroffer you'd have to refuse. The emeritus paragraph is deliberately explicit about the retirement distinction, because naming it yourself is what gets the conversation opened instead of the request quietly denied. Also ask HR to record the separation as **resignation in good standing**, which preserves rehire eligibility and reference language. And send it only after the chair has seen it — being surprised by a resignation letter is how deans become unhelpful.

Now the second half of your question.

The dumpster feeling is grief wearing an accurate-sounding voice. It is measuring your life's work by its continuation in one building, and by that metric every retirement, every move, every death would be a waste — which tells you the metric is wrong, not the life. Your students carry what you taught them into rooms you'll never enter; the papers stay in the literature; and the same attention that made you a scholar is now being spent on a person who will remember, for whatever time she has, that you came. That is not a smaller use of a mind.

Two things worth saying plainly. Caregiving at this intensity has its own exhaustion and its own dark hours, and if it starts to hollow you out rather than tire you, come back and we'll sit with it. And tell one colleague the truth about how hard this is — not the polished version, the real one — because the isolation of the next year will do more damage than the resignation ever could.
